extracted.intended_audience: research funders, peer reviewers, academic policymakers, and researchers interested in research equity
extracted.subtask_short: addressing gender bias in grant review
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and evidence-based recommendations for identifying, measuring, and reducing gender bias in research grant peer review and for complementary institutional policies to promote gender equity in academia.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus review on 'the science' rather than 'the scientist'
rubrics_metrics.description: Instruct peer reviewers to assess the scientific merits of a proposal instead of judging the applicant (the scientist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witteman and colleagues documented a reduction in gender bias by instructing reviewers to focus on the science of a proposal instead of the scientist; this quasi-experimental approach is offered as an actionable intervention that funders should consider following. (Example: change reviewer instructions and scoring rubrics to emphasize proposal content and methods, de-emphasize applicant pedigree or perceived leadership qualities.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect and support research into gender and diversity in academic funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding agencies should launch and fund research into gender and diversity in academic funding and research to better understand bias.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The NIH and European Commission have recently called for research in this area; generating both quantitative and qualitative evidence is important to understand the scale and mechanisms of bias and to design interventions. (Practical note: include calls for proposals, fund empirical studies, and enable data sharing.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Use both quantitative and qualitative evidence to understand bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Combine quantitative data (to measure scale) with qualitative exploration (to understand motivations, incentives, and reasoning) when investigating gender bias in peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Quantitative analysis can detect disparities in scores and funding outcomes; qualitative methods (e.g., interviews, focus groups) reveal why reviewers make biased judgments and how institutional norms shape decisions. The article recommends both approaches to enable effective interventions and sustained change.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implement institutional policies that recognize and counteract gender bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Universities and research institutions must adopt policies to shift traditional gender norms and actively counter gender bias in academia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples include flexible working hours, adequate parental leave, child care facilities, and policies that explicitly recognize and mitigate gendered expectations. Institutional reform should accompany changes in grant peer review processes to address the broader systemic context that produces disparities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tie funding or incentives to institutional gender-equity programs (e.g., Athena SWAN)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use institutional awards or equity program participation as part of funding eligibility or incentives to promote recruitment, promotion and retention of women in academia.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The European Commission draws on the UK’s Athena SWAN initiative; certain biomedical health funding has been tied to Athena SWAN awards, thereby institutionalizing and incentivizing moves toward gender parity. (Implementation: consider conditional funding, scoring, or bonuses tied to demonstrable equity actions.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize and address systemic, historical, and intersecting biases
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that gender bias in grant review is a manifestation of historical and systemic biases within academia and is intersecting with race, class, sexuality, and other markers of difference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patriarchal structures manifest in multifaceted ways; attention should be given to how processes affect women of colour, Indigenous women, and academics from low-income countries, which are underexplored and should be prioritized for study and action. (Anti-pattern: treating gender as a single axis without addressing intersectionality.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware that reviewers may perceive female applicants as less competent or weaker leaders
rubrics_metrics.description: Reviewers often perceive female applicants as less competent or weaker leaders, which can lead to lower scores and reduced funding even when productivity is equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This perception can lead to assumptions about an applicant’s ability to lead multiple projects and thus reduce funding success; reviewer training, explicit criteria focusing on objective measures of proposal feasibility, and blinding where possible can mitigate this. (Evidence: linked study showed women with equivalent past success received lower application scores.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for service-load and 'caring' responsibilities that reduce research time for women
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize that women are often asked to undertake disproportionate service work and bear greater household/caring responsibilities, which reduce time available for research and grant preparation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutions should adopt policies (e.g., workload allocation, recognition of service) to prevent penalizing women for higher service burdens; reviewers and panels should consider contextual factors rather than directly penalizing lower recent productivity without context. (Anti-pattern: assuming equal available research time for all applicants.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Mitigate citation and coauthor recognition biases when assessing productivity
rubrics_metrics.description: Account for documented disparities such as lower citation rates for women, men citing men more, and a 'coauthor penalty' that reduces recognition for women’s collaborative work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluation of productivity should not rely solely on citation counts or authorship patterns without context; panels should be trained to interpret metrics in light of known gendered citation and credit practices. (Example: adjust bibliometric expectations, consider solo vs. collaborative contributions carefully.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Reduce reliance on subjective assessments of leadership capacity that disadvantage women
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid or qualify subjective judgments about leadership and potential to manage multiple grants, since stereotypes about leadership traits advantage men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scoring rubrics should operationalize leadership and management ability (e.g., prior demonstrated project management, institutional support) rather than leaving room for stereotype-driven impressions. (Anti-pattern: vague leadership criteria that enable bias.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitor outcomes and implement corrective measures at the funding-agency level
rubrics_metrics.description: Funding agencies should monitor application scores and funding rates by gender and implement reforms when disparities are detected.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The linked Canadian study demonstrated gendered scoring differences; agencies should routinely analyze their data, conduct quasi-experiments or pilot reforms (e.g., blinded review, revised instructions), and assess impacts. (Practical steps: disaggregate success rates, run interventions like reviewer instruction changes, evaluate effects.)

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize harassment and hostile climates as barriers to participation and career progression
rubrics_metrics.description: Acknowledge that sexual harassment and discriminatory experiences in academic settings hamper women's ability to participate fully and advance, affecting grant success indirectly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-harassment policies, reporting mechanisms, and culture change efforts are necessary complements to peer-review reforms because hostile environments reduce productive research time and opportunities for networking that support grant success.
